item.title: Jevons Paradox Doesn't Apply to Chickens
item.description: More on the relationship between efficiency and welfare
item.content:encoded:
A few months back I published an essay called “Don’t Demonize Efficiency in Animal Agriculture.” In it, I argued that efficiency has important upsides for externality mitigation because the more efficient agriculture is, the less of it you need. To illustrate this point, I argued that if efficiency in the chicken industry had frozen at 1960 levels but demand were held constant, we’d need 3.3 billion more chickens each year to meet today’s demand.

More recently, Martin Gould countered that you can’t hold demand constant when the whole reason demand grew is that efficiency drove prices down. The growth in chicken consumption might itself be a Jevons paradox effect.

Of course Martin is right that I was being hand-wavy in order to point out that the “efficiency = bad” meme is oversimplified and counterproductive. But it’s equally as hand-wavy to observe chicken price going down, chicken production going up, and assume it’s all a Jevons effect.

So I built a model to tease out what’s actually going on. Doing so reinforced my thesis that increasing efficiency has historically been the best way to decrease the number of animals needed for agriculture. But that doesn’t mean that efficiency is always good — the data tells a more nuanced story. If we shift analysis to the perspective of aggregate flock welfare, rather than flock population size, then we can see some of the potential downsides. However, seeing the downsides in this way also clarifies why the techno-optimist perspective is a powerful way to approach farm animal welfare.

How Things Have Changed Since 1960

The first question we’d like to answer is how many fewer chickens do we now need due to efficiency improvements? Previously, my oversimplified method was to look at how chicken size and growth rate have changed, then determine how many chickens-of-the-past would be needed to meet today’s demand.

However, in reality the chicken-of-the-past would be more expensive than today’s chicken, meaning people would eat less of it. How much less is a question of the price elasticity of demand: the increased percentage of chicken that people would consume given a 1% drop in price.

Once we know the price elasticity of demand, then we can more directly answer the question. Since wholesale chicken price is a reasonable proxy for efficiency, we can choose a point in the past, look at the growth rates, size, and price of chicken during that time, use the elasticity to figure out how much chicken would be consumed if it were at that price, then figure out how many chickens at that efficiency would be needed to meet that demand.

The true elasticity of chicken is an economic abstraction that varies significantly by context. However, there have been numerous studies on the topic that give a sense of the range, and it’s sensible to think the aggregate price elasticity since 1960 would fall in that range. The most recent estimate (Luke 2026) puts it between -0.6 and -1.1 (meaning that a 1% decrease in chicken prices leads to a 0.6-1.1% increase in chicken consumption). An older review (Andreyeva 2010) gives -0.44 to -0.92. Lusk 2016 finds larger elasticities up to -2, but using hypothetical purchase scenarios rather than actual transaction data, where price is more salient to respondents than at the register.

In order to be comprehensive and conservative, I considered a distribution of possible elasticities, from -0.44 to -2, centered on -.85. I gave higher-magnitude elasticities less weight since they’re possible but less likely.

I then modeled a comparison between the chicken industry of 1960 versus today. The results are represented by the four charts above:

  • The top left chart represents the range of elasticities considered and their respective likelihood.

  • The top right chart represents how much of the increase in chicken demand is explained by prices coming down — the “Jevons paradox” channel. Compared to 1960, we eat almost seven times more chicken as a country (3.7 times as much per capita) and it costs almost 50% less. In our base case, lower prices only explain 28% of the observed demand, although the possible range is anything from 14-65%. The rest is explained by population growth, income growth, and a secular increase in demand for chicken (e.g., a health-driven pivot away from red meat, product innovation like boneless skinless breasts, etc.).

  • The bottom left chart represents the difference in the number of chickens we need today because of increase in efficiency. In the baseline case, we need 1.2 billion fewer chickens – a 14% decline. That said, if elasticity were at the higher end of the range, we would need more chickens, but 65% of the total probability mass is in the green (and the 1995 analysis below paints a clearer picture).

  • The bottom right chart represents the difference in chicken-days, to capture the shorter amount of time that animals currently spend on farm. In the base case, 229 billion fewer chicken days are needed to meet current demand, although there are some unlikely scenarios in which more chicken days would be needed.

When is less actually more?

This model is an abstraction over a much more complex reality. But there are also more intuitive ways to understand why Jevons paradox doesn’t apply as much to animal proteins.

Firstly, it’s important to understand that a huge part of what consumers pay for animal proteins is retailer margin — these days it’s over half (55%) for chicken. This means that when efficiency changes wholesale price, the signal is heavily diluted by the time it reaches the end consumer.

Let’s consider what this means for a context where we increase efficiency through lowering mortality. A -2 elasticity (the largest found in the literature) means that every 1% drop in consumer price leads to 2% more chicken sold. On the surface, this seems damning for my perspective – if we increase efficiency by 1% by decreasing pre-slaughter mortality by one percentage point, then we might cause 2% more chicken to be produced!

But not so fast – a percentage point drop in pre-slaughter mortality is a 1% decrease in the price of wholesale chicken, which is what the retailers buy. Even if the retailers fully passed this on to the consumer (which they likely wouldn’t), it would translate to a 0.45% decrease in consumer prices, which under our conservative assumptions would increase consumption by 0.9%. And 0.9% more chicken consumed, at 1% better placement productivity, means fewer chicks need to be placed on farms.

This example pertains to mortality reduction, which is the kind of efficiency most aligned with welfare. But it illustrates how it can be possible to achieve both fewer chickens farmed and better welfare, even if total chickens consumed goes up.

Subscribe now

Secondly, let’s think about the canonical examples where Jevons paradox has more dramatic impact. One is the invention of the steam engine, which significantly increased the efficiency of converting coal into power. The resounding success of the steam engine paradoxically increased the total amount of coal consumed. Or, more recently, Jevons paradox has been a topic of discussion in the AI world because there could be an explosion of intelligence-derived work as AI decreases the cost of intelligence.

In these cases, the “paradox” comes from the fact that significant increases in efficiency open up completely new use cases for the resource in question. The steam engine created new demand for power generation in contexts where previously using coal would have been infeasible or uneconomical. AI is changing the fundamental dynamics of how intelligence is used in the economy.

Chicken doesn’t fit that pattern. A 10% drop in chicken price doesn’t open up some previously unreachable use case. In theory, one might expect a Jevons paradox effect if, for example, one kind of animal protein became suddenly cheaper than one of its substitutes (e.g. if pork suddenly became cheaper than chicken we might see demand for pork explode). But chicken is already the cheapest meat at the grocery store. There’s no substitute left to undercut.

Welfare Footprint

I think there’s an important steelman of the anti-efficiency perspective, which happens when we shift perspective to the welfare of individual animals.

The Welfare Footprint Institute is a research group that quantifies animal welfare by measuring hours spent at different intensities of pain, sorted into four categories: annoying, hurtful, disabling, and excruciating. They’ve identified the biggest welfare problems in poultry production and estimated how many hours of each kind of pain those problems generate.

A previous analysis they conducted directly compares the welfare of conventional broilers to broilers in a “reformed” scenario, meaning slower-growing breeds like the Hubbard JA757. The reformed birds experience fewer hours of excruciating, disabling, and hurtful pain than conventional broilers, though slightly more annoying pain because they live longer.

In order to integrate this into our existing model, we have to choose a different year rather than 1960. WFI’s reformed bird grows at about 45g/day, but the 1960 broiler grew even slower than that, which makes direct comparison difficult. However, 1995 was the year in which the conventional broiler of that time grew at a similar rate to today’s reformed birds. So if we run the analysis with efficiency held constant in 1995, then we can more directly compare the welfare of birds now versus then. The comparison isn’t perfect, since today’s reformed birds are purpose bred to have higher welfare, but it’s a start.

Under this analysis, efficiency gains since 1995 mean that we need 1.36 billion fewer chickens and 61.4 billion fewer chicken-days. The difference in chickens needed is positive rather than negative for almost the entire range of considered elasticities, making it different from the 1960 analysis. This is because the source of efficiency gains shifted over time. Between 1960 and 1995, most gains came from faster growth and better feed conversion; after 1995 they came almost entirely from bigger birds — today’s broiler is over 40% heavier than a 1995 one. Bird size is mainly what lowers headcount, since fewer animals are needed per pound of meat.

But looking at aggregate welfare tells a different story. Disabling pain — pain severe enough to interfere with normal function — has gone up by 231 billion hours, a 148% increase over what we’d see at 1995 productivity. Hurtful pain has gone up by 253 billion hours, an 11% increase.

So there might be reasons to worry about efficiency in animal agriculture after all, but they’re not the ones that Martin had in mind. Efficiency most likely decreases how many animals we need in animal agriculture – Jevons paradox doesn’t cleanly apply. But efficiency has also possibly made the welfare of individual animals worse.

At least that’s true at the current technological frontier.

If we further break down the WFI numbers into what’s causing the increased hours in pain, we see a number of discrete issues like lameness, chronic hunger in breeders, heat stress, and ascites. Each of these issues has technological solutions currently in development. Lameness can be mitigated through electron-beam inactivated vaccines, chronic hunger can be addressed through GLP1s or Layers Laying Broilers, ascites and heat stress can be mitigated through CoQ10, and so on.

These technologies are promising because they both improve welfare and raise efficiency — that’s what gives them a path to commercial adoption. If one starts from an anti-efficiency perspective, that might look like a strike against them. But this analysis hopefully shows why this is wrong. The net effect of efficiency has been historically mixed because the upsides (less agriculture) have to be traded off against the downsides (lower welfare per bird). But if we know a technology will directly solve a major welfare issue, then we aren’t faced with this tradeoff. We get less agriculture and better welfare — a Pareto improvement.

In the first essay I ever wrote on this blog, I distinguished between two broad approaches to externality mitigation: degrowth and techno-optimism. When abundance generates externalities, degrowth says sacrifice the abundance. Techno-optimism says innovate your way out of the tradeoff. This analysis gives a more precise way to understand this distinction.

If one thinks the problem with animal agriculture is “efficiency,” then the natural solution is to sacrifice efficiency, leading to degrowth. But once we see that efficiency itself reduces how much agriculture we need, and the actual problem is the downstream effects of efficiency on individual welfare, the question can instead becomes how to mitigate those effects directly. Understanding the nature of the problem ensures we’re pointed at the best solutions.

item.title: Agentic Shopping Makes Conscious Consumerism Actually Work
item.description: A techno-optimist's lens on farm animal welfare.
item.content:encoded:
There’s a certain amount of fatigue around conscious consumerism these days. Do I really have to learn about fabric manufacturing and labor practices in Indonesia to buy a shirt? Do I really need to learn about water management practices in California to buy a bag of almonds?

There are lots of ways in which people have preferences not only about the products they buy, but also about how the products were made. Animal welfare is one example, but people also care about things like labor practices, sustainability, product safety over and above regulation (e.g. microplastics), or even what political tribe the company aligns itself with.

Over the last few decades, modern supply chains have adjusted somewhat to meet this demand for better-made products, and modern consumers have clearly shown a significant willingness to pay for products that align with their values. But conscious consumerism fatigue happens because there’s too much to know about too many companies and industries. And many consumers feel burned after a company they thought they could trust betrays that trust in some way. What people want is for the companies they buy from to just do things better by default.

Companies face the mirror image of the consumer’s problem. I’m confident that there are many people in many businesses trying to find ways to do things better within the economic limitations of their industries. But consumers have a limited ability to tell when a company really is doing better, and therefore a limited ability to reward it. A company can invest heavily in marketing to tell consumers what it’s doing, but marketing is a difficult skill in its own right, entirely separate from the work of actually doing things better. And there’s often little stopping a competitor from making a similar claim without actually doing the hard work.

So we end up in an equilibrium where good actors aren’t fully compensated for creating positive externalities, bad actors engage in “X-washing,” and consumers are left somewhat unsatisfied with their ability to consciously consume. Clearly, there’s room for improvement.

When AI shops

AI agents could change this equilibrium because they remove the attention bottleneck.

As our AI agents become more capable, and learn more about us, one natural endpoint is that a significant amount of consumer purchasing in the future is going to be done through agents. My AI is going to know what I like, and I’ll be able to tell it (or it will just know) that I need new socks, a nice TV for my living room, or a restock of eggs.

This could change the economy in all sorts of ways, but one of the more hopeful outcomes is that it could solve the current problems with conscious consumerism, and make it way easier for companies to be incentivized to do what consumers actually want.

In our current equilibrium, since consumers have so little ability and bandwidth to actually look at what’s going on, businesses don’t have an incentive to report. If almost no one reports, companies that remain opaque look completely normal. A company that discloses more takes on more risk by making its flaws visible, without much reason to think consumers will reward it.

As AI agents start doing more of our purchasing, a new equilibrium could emerge. It begins with companies that are already doing things better surfacing more data and knowing that agents will actually see and understand it. This will become an alternative to brand marketing, or the AI version of SEO. Then, as more companies report and it becomes clear that transparency gets rewarded, the act of non-disclosure itself becomes a negative signal. If it’s known that a company could disclose something positive and benefit from it, but it doesn’t, the natural assumption will be that the company thinks its customers won’t like the answer. Once agents start rewarding transparency, the gravitational pull toward opacity reverses.

Given that AI’s comparative advantage is sifting through mountains of unstructured data, there needn’t be any standardization on what companies report or how they report it. They can just report whatever they think consumers care about, whether that’s price, carbon footprint, or whether upstream suppliers have ever said anything mean about their favorite politician. AI purchases will then reward them in proportion to how well they know their customer, and how they’re doing by their customer’s values.

The hypothesis is that the market for these kinds of premium products will grow when there’s a supply-demand match between what people want, and what companies actually do. Even if AI doesn’t make consumers care more, it could make it much easier for consumers to act on what they already care about without having to pay attention themselves, which would expand the market for products made in specific ways.

From vibes to data

I’ve written before about who captures the welfare premium in the animal product market. Right now, it’s brands like Vital Farms (the second biggest egg brand in the country by revenue), Whole Foods, and ButcherBox that command significant premiums through selling better-made products. The reason these companies are able to capture the premium is because they have consumer trust.

Consumer trust is pretty vibes-based right now, which is out of necessity. The average Whole Foods customer probably couldn’t tell you many specifics about why Whole Foods products are better, they just know that Whole Foods will get them the good stuff.

The market shift I’m describing represents a transfer of trust from brands to AI agents, and the basis of this trust shifts from vibes to data. There are some entities right now that try to provide more data-based trust, like third-party certifiers. But they don’t command premiums, because vibes-based trust is more what the current low-bandwidth consumer demands.

It’s hard to envision what this kind of radical transparency would look like given where we are today, but here is one way to illustrate it. Your agent gets to know you over time. It learns that you care about how animals are treated, along with a bunch of other things, and understands how much you can afford to spend. It can then evaluate products based on how well they match your preferences and budget.

And we’re not just talking about the company or the brand. The information could reach down to the individual product, or even the individual animal. When you buy a chicken breast, your agent could have access to information about the specific chicken it came from: its breeder flock and hatchery, the farm where it was raised, where it spent time within the barn, major events during its life, what it ate, whether it got sick, possibly even biomarkers related to stress, and how it was slaughtered. All this information could be backed up by auditable video footage and other data streams.

This is way more information than the consumer actually wants to know. But the information isn’t for the consumer, it’s for the agent. The consumer gets what they actually wanted, which is to know that their purchases align with their values.

This is pretty different from how supply chains work right now. But much of the physical monitoring infrastructure needed to make it possible, including cameras, sensors, machine vision, and individual animal tracking, is the same infrastructure companies will need to become AI-native anyway. I suspect the hardware transition will begin as part of the move toward Precision Livestock Farming, aimed mostly at improving efficiency and animal health. It will accelerate if and when companies realize that the same data can also give them a competitive edge with consumers.

Some might think that conscious consumerism is a fleeting trend of rich coastal elites and that ultimately this vision fails because people don’t care. Maybe. But I think it’s notable that the richest communities tend to be the ones with the most robust specialty markets. If AI makes us all rich, serving these kinds of consumers will become more important. Plus, I think part of the “people don’t care” story is that caring about which eggs you buy means both spending more money and also becoming an agricultural expert. With AI you just need to spend more money.

The customer is always right?

Some of today’s companies, accustomed to supply chains being opaque, might feel nervous about this vision. Consumers can be crazy and irrational in all sorts of ways, and giving them more say over how supply chains operate gives them more opportunities to shoot themselves in the proverbial feet. But the economist would point out that this new equilibrium is value-creating: it gives more people more of what they want, and it rewards the producers that provide it.

The truly utopian vision is that AI-mediated purchasing can make consumers more rational. Maybe when someone worries that giving a livestock animal a safe, lifesaving drug will make their child autistic, this fear comes from a sense of being kept in the dark over the quality of food going into their child’s body. And maybe once people trust their AIs to actually pay attention, this fear will be put to rest. I don’t know if this will happen. But even if it doesn’t, the company that resents its customers ultimately won’t succeed.

Today, doing things better is only half the battle. The other half is getting millions of busy strangers to notice, and plenty of good companies lose on that half. Once every person has a super-genius in their pocket deciding what to buy, the noticing gets handled. Convincing people you’re a good company stops being a separate activity from being one. What consumers care about and what businesses get paid for become, at last, the same thing. Call it a form of AI alignment.

item.title: My Conversation with Niko McCarty
item.description: An edited transcript from The New Biology podcast
item.content:encoded:
I recently joined Niko McCarty on The New Biology for a wide-ranging conversation about what biotechnology can do for chickens. An edited transcript of that conversation is below. You can watch the full podcast on on Niko’s YouTube channel, or wherever you listen to podcasts.

Why animal welfare needs scalable technologies

Niko McCarty: Today’s guest is Robert Yaman. He’s the founder and CEO of Innovate Animal Ag, a think tank focused on finding high-leverage ways to improve animal welfare while making farming more efficient for producers. My goal in this conversation is to find high-leverage ways that people working in biotechnology can move into the animal-welfare space. Robert, welcome.

Robert Yaman: Thanks for having me.

Niko: Innovate Animal Ag mostly thinks about how to improve the welfare of chickens. About nine and a half billion chickens and 32 million cows are slaughtered each year in the United States, so chickens outnumber cows by roughly 300 to one. Do you focus so much on chickens simply because, from a numbers standpoint, you can improve the lives of vastly more animals?

Robert: That’s definitely part of it. If you look at the land animals we eat each year, something like 97 percent are chickens, and most of the remainder are turkeys and other birds. Even though we eat a lot of beef and pork by volume, the numbers of those animals are relatively small.

There are other factors as well. A layer farm might have a million birds in one place, or even as many as five million. A broiler house might contain 20,000 to 50,000 chickens, and there might be 12 to 16 houses on a single farm. Maintaining good health and welfare is simply much harder when there are so many animals. Technologies that can automate tasks or operate at a larger scale are therefore especially useful for chickens.

The economics are also quite different. The economic value generated by a cow might be $1,000 or $2,000, compared with around $4 for a broiler or $10 to $12 for a layer hen. You can think of that value as the farmer’s health budget for the animal. If you want to keep a broiler healthy, you have at most $4 to do it—and in practice, much less. Finding new ways to improve welfare and productivity matters especially in poultry because the constraints are so much tighter.

Niko: So because a chicken is worth about $4 while a cow is worth $1,000, a farmer has a much stronger economic incentive to save or improve the life of a cow. A vaccine that costs a dollar to administer to a $4 chicken isn’t viable.

To improve chicken welfare and get farmers to adopt an intervention, you have to think about scale from the beginning: What is the cheapest possible way to manufacture and distribute a vaccine? Have those considerations caused chicken and dairy technology to develop in completely different ways?

Robert: Absolutely. Modern dairy farming is very data-driven. Cows often have RFID tags and accelerometers that let farmers track their movement. Milking systems can record how much milk each cow generates every day. Because an individual chicken doesn’t generate the same economic value, you don’t have access to those strategies. An RFID tag might itself cost a couple of dollars, which is most of the health-management budget for a broiler.

Instead, poultry technologies tend to operate at the flock level: How healthy is this group of birds? Does it look as though an infection is breaking out? Should we treat the entire flock?

One thing we think about a lot is how technology could move poultry toward a more individualized paradigm, because ultimately we want every animal to have positive health outcomes and receive appropriate treatment. Individuation is one of the central challenges in poultry welfare, precisely because the economics push so strongly in the other direction.

How chickens were bred for meat and eggs

Niko: You’ve mentioned broilers and layers, the two types of chickens. How much has their efficiency changed, and what has driven that change?

Robert: Before industrial agriculture, chickens were what we would now call dual-purpose. You might have a chicken in your backyard that laid an egg every few days, and if you needed meat one day, you might kill it for dinner.

Modern agriculture split those functions. Broilers are chickens used for meat, while layers are used for eggs. If you think about them as machines—which is a little strange but illustrative—a broiler converts corn and soy into chicken meat. A layer converts those inputs into eggs on a continual basis. The traits you want to optimize are quite different.

Over the last century, those functions have been separated into different breeds. Broilers have been optimized to grow much faster, convert feed more efficiently, and produce more breast meat. Layers have been optimized to lay more frequently, continue laying for longer, and convert feed calories efficiently into eggs.

Niko: How much have they actually changed? How much bigger is a broiler today than it was in the 1950s?

Robert: Modern broilers are roughly three times bigger at slaughter, but they also reach that size much earlier. In the 1920s, a chicken might have been six months old when it was slaughtered. Now it may be four to six weeks old. They are also much more feed-efficient. Depending on how you measure it, the overall productivity improvement is close to an order of magnitude.

On the layer side, a modern hen can lay nearly an egg every day. You might get 300 eggs—and sometimes substantially more—from a single hen. That is perhaps a threefold increase in both the rate and total volume of egg production.

Niko: Can you cross a broiler with a layer, or does that not work?

Robert: They’re still the same species, so I think you probably could technically. I’ve never heard of anyone doing it, though.

Niko: How did people historically select not just for bigger broilers, but for more meat in specific places such as the breast? Are there companies developing these chicken lines and selling them, similar to seed companies selling hybrid crops to farmers?

Robert: It’s almost exactly the same, and I think the breeding strategies were borrowed from, or at least inspired by, the seed industry. These optimizations have come from decades of selective breeding.

The companies that develop the breeds are not generally the companies producing meat or eggs. A breeding company maintains pure lines of highly optimized chickens and crossbreeds them over several generations. Pure lines are crossed to create great-grandparent birds, which are crossed to create grandparents, which are crossed to create parents, which ultimately produce the commercial broiler or layer.

That system serves two purposes. It gives the breeding companies tight control over the genetics, and it protects their intellectual property. You can’t simply take two broilers from a farm, breed them together, and reproduce the same commercial genetics, because those genetics have already been mixed through several generations of crosses.

Share

Does farm efficiency improve animal welfare?

Niko: One thing that makes Innovate Animal Ag interesting is that you’re very explicit about wanting to improve the efficiency of farming so that producers adopt interventions that are also good for animals. You’re trying to improve welfare with farmers, while also improving the economics of farming.

That sounds different from some other arguments in the animal-welfare world. Lewis Bollard of Coefficient Giving has said that, globally, wealth has been heavily correlated with more suffering: as people get richer, they eat far more meat, and more of it comes from factory farming.

Is animal welfare actually worse in wealthier countries? Do wealthier countries necessarily consume more meat, and does that meat necessarily come from lower-welfare systems?

Robert: There’s a lot in that question, and the answer depends on which margin you’re talking about. I often compare this to environmental externalities such as carbon emissions and pollution.

It’s probably true that the dual-purpose backyard chicken we discussed earlier had better welfare than the average chicken on a farm today. In that sense, the industrialization process may have been bad in itself. But if you look at the choices available to us today, there is often much more alignment between efficiency and welfare than people realize.

Take a basic example. Given the conditions of an industrial broiler farm, it is difficult to ensure positive health outcomes for every bird. If a chicken dies prematurely after eating $2 worth of feed, nobody benefits. The farmer loses money, and it is obviously bad for the chicken. If better technology, treatment, or vaccines can improve health outcomes, they reduce waste and improve welfare at the same time.

You could say that industrialization caused climate change because it led us to burn far more fossil fuel. But it doesn’t follow that every improvement in efficiency is bad for the environment. A process that uses less energy to produce the same output can increase efficiency while reducing its carbon footprint. In the same way, it is too simple to say that the drive toward efficiency always makes life worse for animals. Sometimes the two goals are misaligned, but at the current margin they can also be strongly aligned.

Niko: My assumption is that factory farming is here and is unlikely to disappear. Do richer countries eventually consume less meat and demand higher welfare, as we’ve seen to some extent in Europe? Or is that anecdotal?

Robert: I don’t think the relationship is robust enough to make a blanket claim about wealth and welfare. Germany is wealthy, meat consumption is declining, and it has some of the most stringent welfare laws in the world. Japan is also wealthy, but you don’t necessarily see the same trends. There are other factors at play.

It is certainly true that the move toward industrialized agriculture significantly increased meat consumption, and probably made the average life of a chicken worse. But industrialized farming is not going away. There is no realistic path back to preindustrial agriculture while population and meat consumption continue to grow. There are, however, many ways to use new technology to solve some of the problems and negative externalities generated by industrialization. We have to innovate our way forward.

Niko: Do you think chicken welfare has improved over the last decade or two?

Robert: It’s hard to make that claim in the aggregate. Some things are getting better, while others are not.

One result of broilers becoming roughly three times as productive is that we need fewer chickens to produce the same amount of meat. Similarly, one modern layer may be as productive as three layers used to be, so we can raise fewer animals to meet a given level of demand.

But if you look at mortality in the broiler sector—the number of chickens that die before slaughter—the picture is less encouraging. In the 1920s, mortality may have been around 12 percent. It fell significantly over the following decades, reaching perhaps 3.5 percent around 20 years ago, but it has since been rising again. There are several possible reasons, and I don’t think anyone has given a fully compelling explanation.

One factor is the change in antibiotic use. Antibiotics were once widely used as growth promoters and prophylactics. The FDA later tightened its guidance, and many producers have moved toward “no antibiotics ever” programs. There are good reasons for that—antibiotic resistance is a serious problem—but there are also tradeoffs. When antibiotics are used less liberally, bacterial infections can become harder to control.

Niko: When I started learning about animal welfare, I was struck by how often biotechnology appeared to offer a way to improve chicken welfare: breeding, cheaper antibiotics, new delivery methods, vaccines. Yet very few people in biotech seem to work on animal agriculture. Are the human and animal biotech communities simply separate, or do most biotech researchers not realize what they could work on here?

Robert: A big reason is that there isn’t much money to be made in animal agriculture relative to human health. The entire U.S. broiler industry is on the order of $50 billion, and the egg industry is smaller still. Livestock pharmaceuticals are only a fraction of that. If you’re a biotech researcher or entrepreneur, there are many more profitable directions you can go.

That is one reason Innovate Animal Ag exists. There are neglected, relatively low-margin areas with important moral problems and promising technical opportunities. They’re neglected largely because this is not where the money is.

Niko: The entire egg industry is that small?

Robert: Eggs are cheap. Living in the Bay Area, we sometimes forget how extraordinarily efficient the conventional system is. That efficiency is one reason the total market is not very large.

Related: Don’t Demonize Efficiency in Animal Agriculture and Jevon’s Paradox Doesn’t Apply to Chickens.

How the poultry supply chain works

Niko: Before we get into specific technologies, it would help to understand what a hatchery actually looks like. What is the life of a layer chicken? Where does the egg that becomes a layer come from?

Robert: It begins with the breeding pyramid we talked about earlier. The parent birds of commercial layers—called layer breeders—live on farms with males and females, mate naturally, and produce fertilized eggs.

Niko: Are those breeders treated better because they are more valuable? They aren’t being farmed for the eggs we eat; they’re producing the hens that will lay those eggs.

Robert: That’s an important point. They generally have much better health outcomes because they generate much more economic value. If a layer breeder produces 300 commercial hens and each hen is worth around a dollar, that breeder is worth an order of magnitude more than an ordinary layer.

The fertilized eggs are sent from the breeder farm to a hatchery, which is a much more industrial facility. Large racks of eggs sit inside controlled-atmosphere incubators with carefully managed temperature, humidity, and carbon-dioxide levels. Some incubators rock the eggs to mimic what a mother hen would do. A chicken egg incubates for 21 days.

The chicks usually hatch at the hatchery and then go through several processing steps, which may include vaccination, beak treatment, and manual sexing to separate males from females. The day-old female chicks are sent to a rearing farm, where they grow until sexual maturity at around six months. They are then moved to an egg farm, where they may live for another 12 to 18 months.

Niko: The male chicks from layer lines are killed, and the females go to the rearing farm. How do all these separate operations make money?

Robert: Although there are several physical steps, there are generally only two kinds of companies involved. The genetics company owns the breeder flocks and hatcheries and sells young layers to an egg producer. The egg company may own both the rearing farms and the layer farms. The precise arrangement varies, but the supply chain is less fragmented than it first appears.

Niko: Does that concentration make welfare interventions easier to scale? If you persuade one upstream company to adopt something, can it reach a large part of the industry?

Robert: It makes change more “spiky.” The chicken-meat industry, for example, is highly consolidated. A small number of companies produce most of the meat in the United States. That makes each company difficult to move: even a tiny decision can affect billions of chickens, so they pay attention to hundredths of a cent. But if one company does adopt an intervention, you may affect a quarter of the industry at once.

The egg industry is less consolidated, and I think that helps explain why it has seen more product innovation. The egg case contains free-range, pasture-raised, omega-enriched, heritage breeds, blue eggs, and so on. Chicken meat comes in many cuts and formats, but there is less differentiation in how the chickens were raised. More egg companies are competing to distinguish their products, rather than competing almost entirely on cost.

Niko: How is the life of a broiler different from the life of a layer? There should be fewer steps because both male and female broilers are used for meat.

Robert: The supply chains look similar until the final stage. You still have broiler breeders and hatcheries, although meat companies tend to own the breeder farms and hatcheries and buy parent lines from genetics companies.

A broiler’s life is essentially just the rearing phase. They grow for four to eight weeks on the floor of a long barn with feed and water lines, and are slaughtered when they reach the target weight. Layers grow until they begin laying and are then moved into a layer facility. Conventional cage and cage-free systems look different, but layer housing is generally more vertical and includes nest boxes for laying eggs.

Niko: In conventional production, do hens spend their lives in cages?

Robert: Yes, although roughly 40 percent of U.S. production is now cage-free, and states including California have cage-free mandates.

Niko: What does “cage-free” actually mean?

Robert: The hens can walk around inside the barn. They generally live in aviaries, which are vertical structures with several levels. The birds can move among the levels, sleep on perches, and enter nest boxes to lay eggs.

In-ovo sexing to prevent chick culling

Niko: One of Innovate Animal Ag’s biggest projects has been chick culling. In the layer industry, hatcheries manually separate males from females. Only the females go on to egg farms; the males are killed when they are a day old.

Innovate Animal Ag played an important role in bringing a technology called in-ovo sexing to the United States. It determines the sex of a chick before it hatches, so the male eggs can be removed from the process. How did you find the technology, and why did you think it could be economically viable here?

Robert: In biotech, people constantly ask what can be done with the latest technology and what its applications might be. Poultry doesn’t have the same infrastructure for finding and adopting new technologies. The industry changes slowly and in some respects hasn’t changed much in 50 or 70 years.

When I started Innovate Animal Ag in late 2022, I originally intended to build a company that developed an in-ovo sexing technology. I had heard the idea discussed, but I didn’t see the resulting eggs on store shelves, so I assumed important technical problems remained unsolved.

As I did more research, I discovered that the technology already existed. Several companies had commercialized it in Europe, initially driven by legal mandates in Germany and France. But it was also beginning to spread in countries without mandates.

These machines are installed at hatcheries, and each hatchery supplies many farms. A single machine can therefore produce millions or tens of millions of hens a year. Based on the publicly reported capacity at the time, I estimated that perhaps 10 to 15 percent of the European layer flock was already being produced using in-ovo sexing. That was a contrarian view—even people in the egg industry sometimes assumed the technology was confined to a small share of the German market—but it turned out to be significantly further along than most people realized.

Niko: When you say 10 to 15 percent of the market, you mean the number of layer hens that were sexed before hatching—not the number of consumer eggs laid by those hens.

Robert: Exactly. This distinction trips people up. Europe has hundreds of millions of layer hens, and those hens lay tens of billions of unfertilized eggs that consumers eat. In-ovo sexing is performed only on the much smaller number of fertilized eggs that will become the next generation of layers.

Once we understood that the technology was already viable, we shifted from trying to invent it as a for-profit company to asking how a nonprofit could bring it to the United States. The main task was educating the industry that this option now existed.

The technology companies had learned to enter markets through regulatory mandates. The United States offered a different route because we have a robust premium egg market. Vital Farms, for example, became one of the country’s largest egg brands by revenue while selling a high-welfare product at several times the cost of conventional eggs. American consumers are unusually willing to pay for differentiated products and better welfare.

Our thesis was that adoption here didn’t require a mandate. We needed to identify brands whose customers would care, explain the technology, and connect those brands with the European suppliers. We worked closely with NestFresh, the first U.S. producer to adopt in-ovo sexing, and helped troubleshoot the process as it moved forward.

Niko: A natural question is whether the male layer chicks really have no use. Couldn’t they be raised and sold as a specialty or high-welfare meat product?

Robert: Some European companies have done that, particularly during the transition after chick-culling bans took effect. But there are several problems.

First, it is a difficult consumer story. Most people don’t know chick culling exists, and “improve welfare by eating this particular, less desirable chicken” requires a fairly sophisticated explanation. Second, male layers tend to be smaller, tougher, and less appealing as a meat product.

Third, the meat industry has been optimized around birds of specific sizes. Slaughter plants calibrate their equipment to a fairly narrow weight range. Smaller broilers may become rotisserie chickens, while larger birds are processed into breasts and other cuts. Male layers often fall outside those ranges, so the United States does not have much infrastructure to slaughter and process them.

Niko: About 300 million male chicks are culled in the United States each year. How do the available in-ovo technologies identify them?

One approach removes a tiny amount of fluid from the egg and tests it for a sex-linked biomarker. Another uses hyperspectral imaging: instead of collecting only red, green, and blue light, a camera collects many wavelengths and detects the feather color developing inside the egg. It’s fast and noninvasive, but it currently works only for brown-egg breeds. Why doesn’t it work for white eggs?

Robert: Hyperspectral imaging for white eggs is something of a holy grail for in-ovo sexing. Brown eggs are laid by brown hens, and those lines have been bred so male and female chicks develop different feather colors. This made manual sexing easier, and it gives the imaging system a clear signal. White layers don’t have the same visible difference, so researchers need to find another reliable signal.

There are academic projects claiming to distinguish the sexes in white eggs, but sometimes without a convincing explanation of what the model is detecting. That creates a risk that a machine-learning system has overfit its training data. Commercial hatcheries need extremely high accuracy: every female mistakenly removed is lost revenue.

One especially interesting approach is to breed lines in which male and female embryos have different eye colors. If males had red eyes and females had normal-colored eyes, imaging could distinguish them as soon as their eyes developed. But unlike a machine that can simply be installed in an existing hatchery, that trait would have to be bred into the pure lines and propagated through the entire breeding pyramid.

The other existing technologies remain fairly affordable. One uses a molecular assay; another uses imaging to detect the developing reproductive organs. Exact prices aren’t public, but the cost appears to be around $1.50 to $2 per hen. Amortized over 300 or 400 eggs, that is less than a penny per egg—a few cents per dozen. That is modest compared with premiums consumers already pay for cage-free, free-range, or pasture-raised eggs.

Niko: Do egg producers resist even that additional cost? It seems as though they should be able to recover a few cents per dozen by marketing a higher-welfare product.

Robert: In my experience, egg farmers want to do this. Chick culling is something the industry has had to do, not something anyone enjoys. The challenge is aligning the incentives and getting consumers to value the change.

Only about 10 percent of American egg buyers in our surveys could correctly identify what happens to the males. If consumers don’t know the problem exists, it’s hard to charge more for solving it. So far, the U.S. companies that have announced in-ovo sexing—NestFresh, Vital Farms, and Sauder’s—haven’t raised prices because of it. They are treating it as part of the values and identity of an existing premium brand.

Related: You Can Now Buy Eggs from In-Ovo Sexed Hens.

Electron-beams and one-cent vaccines

Niko: Earlier we discussed rising pre-slaughter mortality and the changing use of antibiotics. That brings us to vaccination. What are chickens vaccinated against, how are those vaccines administered, and how do producers think about their cost?

Robert: Avian influenza is a special case with its own set of challenges. For more routine vaccination, the answer differs between layers and broilers.

Broiler vaccines are generally given at the hatchery. Some are administered in ovo: while the embryo is developing, a machine inserts a tiny needle into the egg. That is often effective because it gives the chicken more time to generate an immune response before reaching the farm. Respiratory vaccines may be administered as a spray at the hatchery. Subcutaneous vaccines also exist but are more common for layers.

Because layers live much longer, they receive more health treatments and may be vaccinated again on the farm. A broiler lives only a matter of weeks, while a layer may live 18 to 24 months, long enough for immunity from an early vaccine to wear off.

Niko: Why can’t vaccines simply be mass-administered through water? Why hasn’t the industry optimized every vaccine for the cheapest possible delivery method?

Robert: Some drugs, including many antibiotics, are delivered through water. But there are many diseases a broiler might encounter, and you probably can’t vaccinate a day-old chick against 20 things at once without overloading its immune system. Producers have to prioritize: Which diseases create the highest risk? Which are economically important? Which have effective vaccines available at a viable cost?

That cost constraint is very different from human pharmaceuticals. A human drug may cost a great deal to invent but very little to manufacture; its price can include substantial margin and amortized R&D. For broilers, the full vaccine often needs to cost less than one cent per bird.

Niko: Less than a cent including manufacturing and delivery?

Robert: Yes. That sounds extreme, but hatchery equipment operates at enormous scale. An in-ovo vaccination machine can vaccinate an entire tray of eggs at once, move to the next tray, and repeat continuously.

Marek’s disease is one of the industry’s great vaccination success stories. It was once a severe problem for chicken producers; now nearly every broiler in the country is vaccinated for it at a fraction of a cent per dose. Other diseases have not yet reached that level.

Niko: Innovate Animal Ag’s current work includes an electron-beam technology. My understanding is that you bombard bacteria with electrons, which destroys the genome so the bacteria can’t replicate while preserving the membrane and the antigens on its surface. That could produce a more effective vaccine than inactivating the bacteria with formaldehyde, heat, or other methods.

Why is this needed? Is it cheaper or more scalable than other methods? And what is your thesis for getting it into agriculture?

Robert: The broad thesis is that farmers need more tools to fight bacterial infection. Broad-spectrum tools such as antibiotics create resistance problems, so it would be useful to target the particular bacteria causing trouble on a particular farm.

Electron beams have long been used to sterilize medical equipment and food packaging. A product moves under what is essentially a small particle accelerator and is bombarded with electrons. DNA is among the largest molecules inside a bacterial cell, and the electrons break it apart. The rest of the cell—including the surface proteins that the immune system recognizes—remains largely intact. The bacterium is no longer viable and cannot reproduce, but it presents the immune system with a close facsimile of the real threat.

Suppose a farm has an outbreak caused by a particular strain of Staphylococcus. You take a sample, isolate the strain, grow it in culture, seal the bacteria in bags, and run those bags through the electron beam. You then use the inactivated cells to vaccinate the chickens headed to that farm. When they arrive, they already have immunity to the strain they are likely to encounter.

The general approach is called autogenous vaccination and has existed for a long time. Historically, the bacteria have been inactivated using formaldehyde, heat, or ultraviolet light, which can damage the surface proteins. Preliminary academic data suggest that the less-destructive electron-beam process can generate a much stronger immune response.

Niko: That process sounds as though it would take weeks. If a farm has an outbreak today, it can’t receive a custom vaccine immediately. Is the idea to protect the next flock that arrives on the farm?

Robert: Exactly. A broiler production cycle lasts roughly six to eight weeks, including the period between flocks for cleaning. Our hope at Bulwark Biologics, the company we spun out to develop this technology, is that an outbreak in one cycle can be turned into a vaccine for the next.

The manufacturing process is simple and high-throughput. You grow bacteria—which is well-understood—run them through an electron beam, and administer the resulting material without many additional ingredients. The infrastructure for in-ovo vaccination already exists because of the Marek’s vaccine. We project that the cost could reach about one cent per dose for each bacterial strain.

The business case is straightforward. If a bacterial infection kills 5 percent of the chickens on a farm and each of those birds would have generated around $4 in value, a one-cent vaccine can more than pay for itself.

Niko: So the vaccine would be made at a separate facility and shipped to the hatchery, which already knows which tray of eggs is going to which farm.

Robert: Right. One hatchery often supplies many farms in the same region, and nearby farms may face similar bacterial problems because their environments and microbial communities overlap.

Niko: Do you need enormous scale to make the business viable? Particle accelerators sound like an expensive upfront investment.

Robert: I don’t think the main challenge will be manufacturing economics. Existing electron-beam facilities rent capacity because their machines have such high throughput. Our proposed supply chain uses a vaccine manufacturer located near an existing facility, with the material shipped back and forth.

The harder work will be operational: finding farms with the right problems, matching each farm to the right vaccine, determining the dose, and measuring outcomes. In theory, several bacterial strains could be mixed into one vaccine. But we still need to learn when that makes economic and biological sense. Preventing one strain from growing can sometimes open an ecological niche for another.

Niko: If you receive bacterial samples from farms around the country, Bulwark could also become an observatory for emerging infections. Could those data help identify threats that might eventually affect humans?

Robert: That’s an interesting possibility, although I don’t know how much overlap there is between the bacteria that cause mortality in chickens and those that threaten human health. Salmonella clearly matters for food safety and can also affect birds on farms, but it isn’t the overwhelming cause of poultry-health problems.

Niko: Why not move every hatchery intervention into the egg and eliminate most chick handling altogether?

Robert: Until recently, many things simply couldn’t be done before hatch. In the layer industry, hatcheries already had to inspect every chick to determine its sex. If you’re handling each bird anyway, the marginal cost of vaccination and beak treatment is lower. As we learn to do sexing, vaccination, and other processes inside the egg, it becomes possible to automate much more of the hatchery.

Related: DARPA for Chickens.

Share

Layers laying broilers—and Ozempic for chickens

Niko: Another broiler technology comes from a company called NextHen. Its idea, “layers laying broilers,” is to engineer layer hens—which are very good at producing eggs—to lay eggs containing broilers, which have completely different genetics.

Today, broiler breeders produce the eggs that become broilers. But broilers are much less efficient at laying eggs than layers, and the birds kept alive for breeding can have serious welfare problems because they were selected to grow quickly, not to reproduce comfortably. How does the NextHen technology work?

Robert: You have a breeding pyramid for both layers and broilers, and each breeder normally shares its genetics with its offspring. But that creates a mismatch between the purpose of broiler breeders and the traits for which they were selected.

Layer breeders have been bred to lay many eggs, and that is what we ask them to do. Broiler breeders carry genetics optimized for producing meat, but we ask them to live much longer and lay eggs. That creates both production and welfare problems.

Broiler breeders cannot eat as much as they would like. They have been bred to have a voracious appetite so that they grow very quickly, but if breeding birds were allowed to eat freely, their bodies could not sustain the resulting weight. They are therefore kept on restrictive diets. They may be hungry much of the time, show more aggression, injure one another, and experience high mortality. They are also much less productive. A layer breeder may produce roughly three times as many eggs as a broiler breeder.

NextHen’s approach starts with a layer line that has been gene-edited to become sterile in response to a trigger. While one of these surrogate layers is still developing inside the egg, you inject it with germ cells from a fast-growing broiler line. The adult bird has the body of a layer, but its eggs carry broiler genetics.

Niko: So the chicken itself is a layer, but its germ cells are from a broiler. It is carrying the reproductive genetics of a different line.

Robert: Exactly. You can think of the surrogate as a bird factory capable of producing a different kind of bird. The same underlying technology has also been discussed as a way to preserve endangered or otherwise valuable bird lines. In this application, it resolves the mismatch between broiler-breeder genetics and the job those birds are being asked to do.

Niko: Could it be economically viable? Injecting germ cells sounds like a radical change to the way the industry produces chickens and a major upfront investment.

Robert: The technology is still in development, so it isn’t commercially ready. There are at least two major challenges.

The first is regulation. Approval for gene-edited animals can be lengthy and difficult, even though the chicken consumers would eat would not itself be gene-edited. The edit occurs in the upstream surrogate, while the broiler germ cells and resulting commercial broilers remain unedited.

The second is throughput. Germ cells need to be injected precisely into developing eggs. But the process is conceptually similar to in-ovo vaccination: eggs move down a line, a needle enters each egg at a precise location, and the material is delivered automatically. In principle, it could be cost-effective because replacing broiler breeders with much more productive and healthier layer surrogates creates such large benefits.

Related: The Gene-Editing Platform That Will Transform the Poultry Industry.

Niko: That technology isn’t on the market yet. In the meantime, could we do something else about the chronic hunger experienced by broiler breeders? You’ve written provocatively about “Ozempic for chickens”: giving these birds a GLP-1 drug so they no longer feel as though they are starving.

The GLP-1 peptide is structurally similar in humans and chickens. Could an existing human drug work in birds?

Robert: We know that human GLP-1 peptides can have a similar effect in chickens because researchers have tested them. What we don’t know is whether long-lasting GLP-1 agonists such as semaglutide will work the same way. Chickens have different biology and a different digestive system, so there are still many unanswered questions.

Niko: This seems like an intervention farmers might not want to pay for. The welfare upside is clear, but the economic upside is less obvious. GLP-1 drugs are already expensive and reportedly face manufacturing bottlenecks for human use. Why would producers use them in chickens?

Robert: There could be economic benefits, although they are speculative and we intend to fund research to test them.

The aggressive behavior associated with chronic hunger is itself a production problem. If birds injure or kill one another, the farmer loses output. There is also evidence that reducing stress can improve egg production.

The most interesting potential benefit may appear in the offspring rather than the breeders. Maternal stress can affect the health of broiler offspring. If we make breeders less stressed, we may prevent some of the epigenetic signals that produce worse health outcomes in the next generation. Any small improvement would be multiplied across billions of broilers, potentially creating a significant economic upside.

GLP-1 drugs sound implausibly expensive because the human price is currently so high. But that price mostly reflects margin and amortized R&D, not the cost of the active pharmaceutical ingredient. Imagine that in ten years these drugs are used extremely widely and manufacturing scale has driven their cost down. Poultry might be able to piggyback on the economies of scale created by human medicine. The relevant question for a manufacturer would then be whether the poultry price exceeds the marginal cost of production.

Niko: Unlike an in-ovo vaccine, this drug would need to be given throughout the bird’s life. What delivery problem would have to be solved?

Robert: There are far fewer broiler breeders than commercial broilers. The United States produces billions of broilers but only tens of millions of breeder birds, so the scale is more manageable than it first appears.

Still, humans inject these drugs weekly or take a pill every day, neither of which maps neatly onto poultry production. One possibility is a slow-release subcutaneous implant that lasts for much of the chicken’s life; companies are already exploring similar approaches for dogs and cats. Another is an oral formulation delivered through drinking water.

One uncertainty is the drug’s bioavailability in chickens. Their digestive system differs from ours; food sits in a crop before reaching the stomach. We don’t know whether that would make oral delivery better or worse. There is also evidence that broilers’ unusually strong appetite may be related to naturally low GLP-1 levels. If so, even modest supplementation could make a difference.

Related: Ozempic for Chickens.

Niko: A theme of this conversation is that, because each chicken is worth so little, welfare interventions have to operate at enormous scale. You automate them at the level of the egg, deliver them through water, or treat the whole flock.

Stripe and several other companies recently announced the Intercept initiative, a $500 million effort to develop broad-spectrum prophylactics and environmental systems that reduce infectious disease in humans. Could a similar approach help chickens? Why don’t farms use large-scale pathogen-sterilization systems?

Robert: We used to have broad-spectrum prophylactics for chickens: antibiotics. Most chickens received them, and now many do not. That creates an opportunity to ask what could replace some of what antibiotics accomplished without creating the same resistance problem.

There is an interesting overlap with Intercept’s interest in technologies that can safely reduce pathogens in the air. Far-UVC light is one example; glycol vapors are another. Both could potentially reduce the pathogen burden inside a poultry barn.

We hope to study agricultural applications of these technologies over the next several years. Far-UVC is currently probably too expensive for agriculture. But if efforts such as Intercept lead to lamps being installed in hospitals, airports, and schools, manufacturing scale could eventually make them affordable for barns. Again, poultry may be able to benefit from a technology and cost curve created for human health.

Precision farming and the Accelerator Farm

Niko: Is there an end state in which, even though chickens aren’t worth much individually, we can use extremely high-precision agriculture in a way that remains economically valuable for farmers? What would that look like?

Robert: We think a lot about the optimal method of chicken production: a system that is economically viable while also optimizing for welfare. Could pre-slaughter mortality in broilers fall to 1 percent, or as close to zero as possible?

I think about poultry health as analogous to human health. We have made huge improvements in our ability to produce positive health outcomes for people over the last 60 years, but people still suffer and die of diseases. Progress is iterative: we identify the biggest problems, work hard to solve them, and then turn to the next ones. That is the vision I have for poultry welfare. As technology improves and societies become wealthier, I think we can solve many of the major problems.

Niko: We recently went on a walk, and you described your utopian vision for the chicken farm of the future. What does that farm look like?

Robert: A major part of it is moving from flock-level management and treatment to individualized management.

Imagine you were a doctor treating a patient, but the only information you had was public-health data from the town where that patient lived. You could do something useful, but your treatment would not be very precise. Poultry producers are in a similar position today.

Better monitoring, machine vision, individual tracking, and targeted treatment could eventually make the $4 health budget of each broiler go much further. The goal would be to make sure that every chicken on a farm has a positive health outcome.

Many people view animal agriculture as a dark and frightening system they would prefer not to examine too closely. But by combining these technologies, I think we can reach a point where industrial agriculture is much more closely aligned with our values.

Niko: We’ve also talked about AI agents acting on behalf of consumers. An agent could potentially query farm data and verify that someone is buying a genuinely higher-welfare product instead of merely trusting a label. Consumers might be willing to pay more, particularly in wealthy countries, which would increase the health budget available for each chicken. What would that system look like?

Robert: We focus both on concrete improvements we can make now and on the long-term direction of the industry. So far we’ve mostly discussed how AI, new technology, and increased wealth could change production. But the demand side could change too.

Consumers already pay a significant welfare premium for some animal products. Vital Farms has built a large customer base willing to pay $6 to $12 for a dozen eggs. That happens even though consumers have limited visibility into what is occurring on any particular farm. They have to trust that a company or certification represents their values.

AI agents can process much larger amounts of information than a human standing in a grocery aisle. Imagine a future in which farms are far more transparent, their welfare and health data are available, and producers who do better can actually get paid for it.

Farmers often tell me, “We could do this better, but no one will pay for it. Our competitors who don’t make the investment will beat us on price.” Better data could create a race to the top: consumers could buy products that genuinely match their preferences, while producers could capture the value of better practices.

Getting there would require much more transparency throughout the supply chain, along with tools that can interpret the data and distinguish real performance from marketing claims.

Related: How to Make Precision Livestock Farming Useful for Poultry.

Niko: Much of what you work on depends on other people taking action. You can research and write about an intervention, but ultimately you need a producer such as Vital Farms to adopt it. Why not build a prototype farm that combines all of these ideas and demonstrates a viable model for the future?

Robert: We are doing that. I’m glad you asked, because I don’t think I’ve talked about it publicly yet—so this is a New Biology exclusive.

One of our biggest new projects is creating a place where these ideas can be tested and proven. The poultry industry hasn’t changed much in the last 50 to 70 years, and its muscle of innovation has atrophied. In other sectors where meaningful innovation happens, there is usually a place where innovators can test things, iterate quickly, make adjustments, and combine different technologies.

We’re building what we currently call the Accelerator Farm. It will be a commercial broiler facility that sells chickens into the market, but it will also be a place where startups can test technologies and where we can combine interventions.

For example, we could install far-UVC lights alongside the electron-beam vaccine and see whether together they reduce bacterial loads to very low levels. We hope to demonstrate some of these larger ideas while also helping companies optimize their technology before pitching it to other farms. By the time they approach a conventional producer, they should already understand the practical bottlenecks.

Niko: What does a facility like that cost? It presumably isn’t trivial for someone to enter the market as a new broiler producer.

Robert: One thing that gives us flexibility is that Innovate Animal Ag is a nonprofit funded by philanthropy. I don’t expect the farm to be highly profitable, at least in the short term. We may eventually find a model that produces better welfare and is also more efficient. But initially we will invest substantial money in experimental equipment, and if a test goes poorly and we need to cover lost margin, philanthropic funding can absorb that risk.

Niko: Where will the Accelerator Farm be based?

Robert: We don’t know yet. We’re still figuring that out.

Niko: Is Innovate Animal Ag hiring? I know you hire program directors to lead different areas of work.

Robert: Yes. We’re growing quickly and hiring program directors for several of our core efforts, including in-ovo sexing, the electron-beam vaccine, and the GLP-1 work.

Our model is inspired by DARPA. Each program director owns a portfolio, designs the interventions, and becomes an expert in the domain. That is a persistent hiring need for us.

The Accelerator Farm will also be a significant operation. We’re hiring both a head of research and a head of operations for that project. If this kind of work interests you, we’d love to hear from you.

Niko: Robert, thanks so much for coming on the podcast.

Robert: Thanks for having me. This was really fun.

item.title: How We Get the Farm of the Future
item.description: Corporations are the original agents, and agentic purchasing can align them
item.content:encoded:
A while ago I wrote about what the “chicken farm of the future” might be like (see parts 1 and 2). The purpose of that exercise was to try to envision how far we could push animal welfare in a world of abundant wealth. What could we build if AI makes everything affordable and possible?

My first stab was pretty weird by today’s standards: each chicken would live its whole life in a single comfortable location, endure no handling or transportation, and have its basic needs and healthcare provided automatically through robotics and AI.

A year and a half later, I wouldn’t necessarily stand by every detail. But the point is that if AI delivers on the promise of providing massive abundance across society, we need a vision for how to convert that wealth into a husbandry system that’s as good as money can buy for welfare, sustainability, and everything else we care about.

What I left handwavy was how that would actually happen. I assumed that if a better farm was something society wanted and could afford, it would get built. But of course things don’t always work that way, as evidenced by the current disconnect between the kinds of farming practices most people find acceptable, and what we actually have today.

After writing last month about how agentic shopping could push the supply chain towards more transparency, I now understand what the path will look like. It first involves moving from a supply chain built on trust, to one built on verification, which agentic purchasing enables. Then, it’s a matter of letting economic growth and technological advancement run their course.

Why it’s hard to buy what you want

When I previously wrote about how agentic shopping can push the supply chain towards greater transparency, I think I did a bad job explaining why I find the idea so powerful. It’s not a matter of making it a little easier for wealthy people to consciously consume. It’s about making it possible for the supply chain to reliably deliver the things people actually want.

When people buy food, they want a lot of things at once. They want it to be safe and healthy, taste good, be easy to prepare, be good for the environment and for animals, come from companies that treat their workers well, and be as cheap as possible. Some of these traits are easily verifiable. The price is on the sticker, making it easy to optimize for.

Many of the other traits are based on trust. Companies make marketing claims, and some pay third parties to certify them. But no matter how thoughtful a shopper is, they have no way of knowing what actually happened in the supply chain behind the specific product in their hands.

Why are things this way? Fundamentally, it comes down to attentional bandwidth. People don’t have time to pay attention to every aspect of every product they buy, so companies have little reason to tell them. If shoppers did pay attention, companies might disclose a lot more and be rewarded for it. But realistically, how many people would read those disclosures, and how many could make sense of them?

So the equilibrium is that companies disclose relatively little, and consumers pick a brand they trust to deliver what they want.

Trust can be well earned, and certainly there are many companies genuinely trying to do things better, so this setup does work to a certain extent. But it also creates some distorting incentives:

  • Signals are fakeable - Winning consumer trust is largely a matter of marketing and branding, which is a different skill from running an operation consumers would like if they were fully informed. A company that runs a great operation but is bad at marketing will lose in the marketplace. More worryingly, a company that’s good at marketing but runs a mediocre operation can win, and consumers have little ability to tell.

  • Claims must be easily understandable - Marketing claims push towards traits that are easy for consumers with limited bandwidth to quickly understand. A consumer might want sustainability and welfare claims to be science-backed, but how would they know unless they were a scientist themselves? Instead, claims are boiled down into lossy proxies like “organic,” and “free-range.” A claim like “This chicken was given GLPs because it shares genetics with fast-growth broilers and, as a result, is often needlessly hungry” would never work on a package.

Certifications try to solve these problems by taking on the evaluative process themselves. In theory, they’re independent, and they can bring a scientific lens to what they’re certifying. But ultimately they face the same challenges as brands:

  • They must themselves win consumer trust, and that trust is just as fakeable for certifiers as it is for brands. A certification guides purchases by letting consumers feel good about them, and a lenient certification can do that just as well as a strict one.

  • Their own program must also be compressed into something that’s easy for consumers to understand. However much science goes into the standard, it comes out the other end as a thumbs up or thumbs down, removing any incentive to improve beyond the standard. Suppose a certification earns a producer a premium if their mortality rate is at most 5%. Getting from 6% to 5% gets the premium, but getting from 4% to 3% earns nothing extra, even though that improvement is equally important for welfare.

    A more complex certification like Global Animal Partnership could have a tiering system with scores 1 through 5. But given a “3,” a consumer is left wondering whether they can feel good about the purchase, and they’re back to being expected to do research they’re unlikely to do.

These distortions mean that there’s an upper limit on how much the supply chain is capable of meeting consumer demand for welfare. Even shoppers with the money and the willingness to pay have no reliable way to buy what they want. In fact, I would claim that today, we know a lot about what constitutes good welfare, and we know many ways to improve welfare that are affordable to consumers. But the supply chain just isn’t set up to reliably reward companies for doing them.
