Alignment through verification

There’s an interesting analogy here to AI alignment. In the most general sense, an “agent” is some entity that does something on my behalf. It’s “aligned” if it acts in accordance with my preferences and values. Companies that provide products to consumers are, in a way, the original agents. I ask the corporation-as-agent for a carton of eggs, and it acts on my behalf to breed the hens, raise them, collect and package the eggs, and get them to my store.

We don’t currently know how to reliably align AI agents. An agent asked to book a fitness class might do it by hacking into the gym’s system and bumping someone else off the list. Similarly, we don’t yet have the capability to align corporations-as-agents. I can tell one to “get me some humanely raised eggs,” and the eggs will arrive. But because of the distortions above, I have no way to make sure they were produced the way I’d want.

I believe AI purchasing will help to better align corporations, not by controlling them directly, but by letting customers send more specific preferences into the supply chain, incentivizing more aligned behavior.

The compression and simplification of the signals around welfare is a function of humans having limited attentional bandwidth. AIs don’t have this problem. They can inspect large amounts of data and understand the entire corpus of scientific research. Instead of trusting companies to do the right thing, they can verify through data that the right thing was done.

This can solve the problem of fakeable signals. Marketing is all about competing for attention when attention is scarce. When AI makes attention abundant, the role of marketing changes, perhaps to demonstrating as robustly as possible that your product is the thing that people want.

It also can solve the problem of claims needing to be understandable, although in a more indirect way. Agents can make sense of science and data far better than most people. But I doubt people will want their agents to explain it all to them. People want to end up with something that meets their product specifications, and that they also feel good about, but that they have to think about as little as possible. Right now the only way to do that is to trust a label. An agent offers another way: it thinks about the details so you don’t have to.

In a world of agentic purchasing, the consumer is still operating on trust. But the trust is instead given to the agent, rather than the brand. Assuming that the labs in Silicon Valley do their jobs correctly, the agent will actually be aligned to my values and interests more so than the corporation ever could be. For example, if your agent is truly aligned to you, it would know to buy you eggs that don’t involve chick culling, even if you never said explicitly that you found it objectionable, and perhaps even if you don’t know what chick culling is.

So in the future, when I ask my AI to buy me a carton of eggs, there will be a stack of agents acting on my behalf. Some will be AIs, and some will be corporations with human, robotic, and digital agents of their own. The goal is for that stack to be aligned from top to bottom. Despite the mind-boggling complexity of a long industrial supply chain, it will be as if I did each part myself. Except I won’t have to do, or think about, any of it.

We can have Dyson Spheres but not nice farms?

Corporate alignment is one thing, but the farm of the future as I’ve described it is something further. It envisions something beyond our current technological capability, and far beyond something most people could afford. A transparent and responsive supply chain can provide welfare up to the point that consumers care and are willing to pay, but it can’t change the fact that most consumers today might want the cheapest option.

The difference is that a trust-based supply chain has a fixed ceiling on how much welfare it can deliver, while a transparent and aligned supply chain’s ceiling rises with whatever people want and can afford. And AI is likely to raise it in a few ways:

  • First, if AI delivers on the promise of material abundance, willingness to pay will go up for traits outside of price. The cost of welfare as a share of real income will go down, making the tradeoff consumers constantly face less of a tradeoff.

  • Second, if AI delivers on the promise of technological advancement, the cost of welfare will go down, through advancements in many of the technologies I write about on this Substack.

  • Third, the supply chain will be able to track consumer preferences and societal values as they change over time. If greater material abundance increases concern for animal welfare, a transparent and aligned supply chain allows for this care to easily translate to better welfare outcomes.

People at the frontier of AI talk seriously about a world where AI cures all disease, and economic growth ends material scarcity. If we’re willing to entertain that world, it’s surely not much of a stretch to imagine farms where animals have a better quality of life than they would in nature, and where their needs are met as fully as we know how. What I’ve described here is how I believe we’ll get there.

I think the power of transparency and verification to align institutions that are currently misaligned goes well beyond animal agriculture. I hope that as AI gives us the tools to deeply interrogate every aspect of our society, a new norm of transparency will emerge, giving us more control over what kind of society we build. The story of history since the industrial revolution has been about fighting poverty and material scarcity, and in that fight some tradeoffs had to be made. Now as we emerge victorious in that old war, we’ll have the ability to decide which of those debts we want to start paying back.
